chunks: Gold versus copper for PCB conductors. The question: What are the tradeoffs of using gold vs copper on the conduction layers?
Copper carries the current on a circuit board. Gold appears only as a very thin coat on the pads, the bare spots where parts are soldered.
Gold is not a better conductor than copper (it resists current about 1. 45 times more), and it costs thousands of times more per gram.
What gold does well is resist corrosion, so the pads stay clean, flat and easy to solder.
Picture a steel beam in a bridge with a thin coat of rust-proof paint. The beam does the real work, and the paint just protects it.
On a board, copper is the beam and a gold layer about 0. 1 µm thick is the paint. Underneath sits a thin layer of nickel that stops the copper from creeping into the gold.
The analogy is loose on one point: the gold dissolves into the solder during assembly, so it protects the pad only until then.
An ENIG-finished pad in cross-section (not to scale). Copper carries the current. A few microns of nickel stop copper diffusing into the gold. A gold layer of only about 0.
1 µm keeps the nickel from oxidising until soldering, when it dissolves into the molten solder and the solder bonds to the nickel.
Resistivity: how much a material resists current, whatever its shape. Gold is 2. 44 and copper 1. 68, in units of 10 to the -8 ohms·m ("Best conductor material for PCB layers").
Noble metal: a metal such as gold that does not rust or tarnish. ENIG: electroless nickel, immersion gold.
A common pad finish with a very thin gold layer over nickel ("PCB layers and their materials"). Embrittlement: weakening of a solder joint when too much gold dissolves into it.
Make the same trace out of both metals. Gold resists 2. 44 / 1. 68 = 1. 45 times more, so to match 35 µm of copper you would need about 51 µm of gold.
Even a gold layer only as thick as the copper, 35 µm over 100 cm², weighs about 6. 8 g, against 3. 1 g of copper. At roughly USD 100 per gram, that gold costs hundreds of dollars.
The ENIG finish uses only about 15 mg over the same area. That is the whole idea.
"Copper for the conductors, gold only as a thin finish.
Gold is actually a worse conductor, about 45% higher resistivity, and thousands of times more expensive per unit mass, so gold traces make no sense.
Its advantage is that it's noble: it doesn't oxidise, so pads stay solderable and contacts stay low resistance. That's why we use ENIG, nickel with about 0.
1 micron of gold, and gold-plated edge connectors. Downsides are softness, it dissolves into solder and can embrittle joints above a few percent, and the nickel adds loss at GHz."
